paper_title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the process is often slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity. We present SwarmEvolve, a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents' hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Many problems in mathematics and scientific computing can be framed as search for good program. Examples include symbolic regression, optimizing constants in inequalities, and building robust solvers 1 SwarmEvolve for differential equations. This search can be carried out through evolutionary computation, method to iteratively improve candidate programs through variation, crossover, and selection [32, 39]. Recently, LLMs have been used as the mutation and crossover operators in such evolutionary processes [43, 49, 73]. These LLM-guided frameworks have made strong progress on many open problems. In particular, FunSearch found new cap set constructions [54], and AlphaEvolve found more efficient algorithm for multiplying 4 4 complex matrices [50]. Later work applied this approach to solve many more problems in mathematics and computer systems [24, 20, 12]. These frameworks differ mainly in how they explore. FunSearch evolves programs on separate islands, and AlphaEvolve and its open-source variants add MAP-Elites archive to keep diverse programs [59, 1, 37]. To save LLM calls, some methods reject nearduplicate proposals, adaptively allocate the search budget, or evolve the search strategy itself [42, 10, 46]. Others guide exploration with better context, such as how past changes affected the score, related literature, simulated peer review, or solver split into separate steps [34, 45, 78, 40]. Recent work also scales up the search. Some methods run many parallel trajectories [77] or train the LLM on each problem with reinforcement learning [79, 64, 70]. Others use more agents with different roles, such as an ensemble of frontier LLMs in AlphaEvolve, multi-agent debate, and coding agents that coordinate through shared memory or an orchestrator [35, 52, 69]. When agents build on one anothers findings, they have produced new results on open problems [9, 7]. These works suggest that diverse proposals, crosspollination of ideas, and iterative refinement are key to new discoveries on open scientific problems. Yet in most of these frameworks, the search is slow and expensive. Each agent writes long chain of thought in text. The growing solution archive, evaluator feedback, and text messages between agents make the LLM context very long. Scaling to many agents, larger models, or test-time training multiplies this cost. As result, the search cannot run at the scale that many open problems need. We therefore ask: (cid:17) Can swarms of low-cost agents make evolutionary search faster and better? We present SwarmEvolve, an evolutionary search framework in which swarms of low-cost latent agents reason in latent space and communicate by passing KV caches. It builds on recent work on latent reasoning, where an LLM reasons with continuous vectors instead of sampled tokens [29, 80, 60, 74, 82], and on latent communication, where LLMs exchange token embeddings [51], activations [53], hidden states [81, 19, 84], or KV caches [61, 23] instead of text messages. In particular, LatentMAS combines both without training. Its agents reason in latent space and pass their KV caches to summarizer that writes the answer [85]. We use this mechanism as the basis for large-scale, low-cost evolutionary search. Because latent reasoning and communication are cheap, SwarmEvolve runs hundreds of agents in each round of evolution. The agents form distinct swarms, and each swarm has its own focus, such as implementing construction from the literature or using textbook method. Inside swarm, each agent reasons from its unique perspective for 40 latent steps. novelty filter then keeps the agents in each swarm whose latent reasoning trajectories are farthest apart in cosine distance. Finally, each swarms summarizer agent reads the KV caches of the kept agents and writes one new program. Compared with existing frameworks, SwarmEvolve has three advantages: 1. Greater diversity. While existing methods generate one response at time or run small team of agents, SwarmEvolve runs 450 latent agents per round, each with different specialization, parent program, and way of thinking, and so samples far more diverse proposals. 2. Built-in crossover. SwarmEvolve recombines ideas directly in latent space. summarizer agent reads the KV caches of agents that studied different parent programs and writes one program that combines their ideas. 3. Higher throughput. Since agents do not decode or encode text between steps, SwarmEvolve evaluates 5 to 13 times more programs per hour than existing SOTA frameworks and reaches their 60minute scores in median of 3 to 8 minutes. We compare SwarmEvolve with OpenEvolve, ShinkaEvolve, and CodeEvolve on 21 problems from mathematical discovery and scientific computing. Each framework runs with Qwen3 8B, 14B, and 32B-FP8 [75] 2 SwarmEvolve for 60 minutes on one GPU (Figure 1). SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score with all three models. With Qwen3 8B, it scores higher than all three baselines with Qwen3 32B-FP8. After only 15 minutes, it already scores higher than the 60-minute averages of all baselines with every model. On three problems, SwarmEvolve with frozen Qwen3 8B also improves on the constructions that AlphaEvolve originally found with frontier Gemini models. These results suggest that swarms of low-cost latent agents are fast and scalable way to use AI for open mathematical and scientific discovery.

sections.content: LLMs usually reason by decoding chain of thought in text [71, 38]. In latent reasoning, the LLM instead feeds the last hidden state ht back as the next input embedding et+1, so it reasons in its continuous embedding space without sampling tokens [29, 80, 83]. sections.title: 3 SwarmEvolve
sections.content: SwarmEvolve is an evolutionary search framework that runs latent-reasoning agent swarms to improve It keeps an archive of all candidate programs, together with their scores programs over many rounds. and evaluation feedback. In each round, it selects parent programs from the archive for refinement and crossover. The search requires an initial program, which is usually simple baseline solution. As illustrated in Figure 2, each round consists of the following steps. Form swarms. To start round, SwarmEvolve forms 10 swarms of 45 latent agents each. All agents in swarm share one main focus. Each agent receives distinct prompt, which combines one of five phrasings of this focus with one of nine ways of thinking, such as reasoning from first principles or reconsidering assumptions (Supplementary Table 4). Each swarm also receives set of parent programs, which are assigned to its agents in turn so that each agent reads exactly one program. The 10 swarms are of four types: Four refinement swarms each receive one of the two best programs in the archive, with two swarms per program. Each swarm takes the main focus used least often so far for its program, such as its mathematical formulation or its use of the time budget. Their goal is to improve the best programs. Three hybridization swarms each receive five programs drawn at random from the ten best, so nine agents read each program. Their goal is to combine the strongest ideas into one new program. Two exploration swarms each receive four programs drawn at random from the entire archive. Nine agents read each program, and the other nine agents read only the problem statement with no parent program. Their goal is to explore less considered directions. One fresh-start swarm receives only the initial program. Its goal is to find new approach that differs from existing ones. Reason in latent space. Each latent agent reads the problem statement, its focus prompt, and its assigned parent program with the programs evaluation results. It then takes 40 latent reasoning steps. sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We compare SwarmEvolve with three state-of-the-art frameworks: OpenEvolve [59], ShinkaEvolve [42], and CodeEvolve [1] on 21 problems from five domains (Appendix D). Sixteen of these problems, in packing, geometry, analysis, and combinatorics, come from Appendix of AlphaEvolve [50]. For these problems, we use the same problem statements, initial programs, and evaluators from OpenEvolve. The score of each problem is its objective value divided by that of the construction published by AlphaEvolve, so score above 1 improves on AlphaEvolve. We also design five scientific computing problems on sparse linear systems, eigenvalues of non-normal matrices, and the Burgers, convection-diffusion, and Helmholtz equations, whose score is the number of correct digits relative to high-fidelity ground truth, averaged over challenging test cases with various parameters or matrices. Problem details are given in Appendix D. Each framework is given 60 minutes on one GPU with 8 CPU cores that evaluate 8 programs in parallel. The three baselines keep their default configurations, let the model reason in text before it answers, and serve it with vLLM [41] for fast inference. Every framework runs three seeds on every problem with each of Qwen3 8B, 14B, and 32B-FP8.

sections.title: 4.2 Latent space analysis
sections.content: Latent agents make the reasoning of swarm directly measurable and fast to filter numerically. In this section, we analyze how the reasoning trajectories of the swarms are spread across latent space. Figure 5 shows one round of circle packing problem with Qwen3 8B. It projects the centered and normalized mean hidden states of the latent agents onto their first two principal components. On the left panel, agents of the same swarm lie close together and apart from other swarms, so each focus clearly moves its swarm to its own region of latent space. In this example, the first principal component roughly orders the swarms by role, from the refinement swarms to the exploration and fresh-start swarms. On the right panel, within swarm, the agents form clusters by the parent program they read. The novelty filter keeps agents from every cluster and covers the swarm roughly evenly. The focus prompts and the novelty filter therefore give each round proposals that differ both across swarms and within each swarm, leading to diversity in the search process. 8 SwarmEvolve Figure 5: Mean hidden states of the latent agents for circle packing problem with Qwen3 8B, projected onto their first two principal components: the 450 latent agents of all 10 swarms with the swarm centers (left), and the 45 latent agents of one exploration-focused swarm, each reading different parent programs (right). The swarms occupy distinct regions, and the novelty filter keeps latent agents from every cluster.

sections.title: 5 Discussion
sections.content: SwarmEvolve shows that evolutionary search can be fast, cheap, and strong at the same time. Latent agents skip the slow step of writing text, so one GPU can run hundreds of agents in each round. With the same model and the same time budget, SwarmEvolve evaluates many more programs than text-based frameworks, reaches their final scores early in the run, and ends with higher scores. Even with small openweight LLM, it improves on several constructions that AlphaEvolve found with frontier LLMs. Latent reasoning is key part of this gain. When we replace the latent reasoning steps with text reasoning, the scores drop (Appendix A.1), even when the agents are given higher text token budget than the latent token budget. Longer text makes each round slower, so the search evaluates fewer programs in the same time and ends with lower scores. Latent reasoning gives each agent enough room to think while keeping each round short. Scaling the number of agents in swarm also helps to improve the framework performance early in the search (Appendix A.2). Since larger swarm studies each parent program from more perspectives, each round explores more of the design space initially. This early advantage matters most when each evaluation is expensive, such as large simulation in science or engineering, where only few programs can be evaluated. Later in the search, swarms of different sizes reach similar scores, while scaling to larger, more intelligent LLMs still raises the final score consistently. More broadly, SwarmEvolve makes large-scale search for new programs affordable on single GPU. This opens the method to many problems in mathematics and scientific computing. In mathematics, swarms can search for new constructions and proof strategies. In computing, they can improve algorithms for speed and accuracy. In scientific computing, they can write better PDE solvers, discover formulas through symbolic regression, and design more efficient numerical methods. Many of these problems have clear evaluators or desired outcomes, such as higher accuracy or faster speed, which is what evolutionary search needs. SwarmEvolve has three limitations. First, all latent agents and summarizers share one LLM, because summarizer can read the KV caches of its agents directly only when they come from the same model. SwarmEvolve Learned translations between the KV caches of different models [23] could extend SwarmEvolve to swarms whose agents run different models. Second, our implementation requires LLMs with standard attention. Linear-attention, state-space, and hybrid models compress the past into fixed-size state [36, 27, 76], so latent communication between them needs way to merge the states of several agents. Third, the memory for the KV caches of round grows linearly with the number of agents, the number of latent reasoning steps, and the number of layers, so the largest LLM we test needs large GPU. Compressed latent messages [11] and rounds spread over several GPUs could let SwarmEvolve scale to larger models and longer runs.

sections.title: 6 Summary
sections.content: We introduce SwarmEvolve, an evolutionary search framework in which swarms of low-cost agents reason in latent space and communicate by passing KV caches. This design lets one GPU run hundreds of agents in each round, so the search explores much more of the design space in the same time. On problems from mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve finds better programs faster than textbased frameworks, and with small open-weight LLM it improves on several results that AlphaEvolve found with frontier LLMs. These results show that large-scale search for new mathematical constructions, algorithms, and scientific computing methods does not necessarily need frontier models or large compute budgets. Swarms of small latent agents can make this kind of AI-driven scientific discovery fast, cheap, capable, and widely available.

sections.title: A Ablation and Scaling Studies
sections.content: A.1 Replacing Latent Reasoning with Text Reasoning Using Qwen3 8B, we replace each agents 40 latent reasoning steps with text reasoning of up to 40 tokens, which matches the latent budget, or up to 256 tokens, which is enough for short paragraph. The summarizer receives this text in its prompt. Latent reasoning gives the highest average score after 60 minutes, 0.804, against 0.796 and 0.767 for 40 and 256 tokens of text reasoning (Supplementary Table 1). Text reasoning is much slower. With 256 tokens, the agents of round take about 32 seconds to write their text reasoning, against only about 4 seconds for 40 latent reasoning steps. The summarizers then encode the text of their agents, which adds 8 seconds per round with 40 tokens and 15 seconds with 256 tokens. In 60 minutes, SwarmEvolve therefore evaluates 734 programs with latent reasoning, more than the 663 and 402 with 40 and 256 tokens of text reasoning. Specifically, text reasoning with 40 tokens scores higher than text reasoning with 256 tokens. This is potentially due to longer reasoning messages overwhelming the 32,768-token context window of the summarizer. This suggests that agent swarms can efficiently communicate with short messages, and latent reasoning and communication are more efficient than text. The novelty filter keeps two thirds of them, so each summarizer reads 0, 10, 30, or 50 latent agents. In the case of 0 latent agents, the summarizer reads the problem statement and all programs of its swarm, the union of what the latent agents would read. Each setting runs three seeds with the setup of Section 4. Larger latent teams raise the score most early in the search (Supplementary Figures 1 and 2). Over the first 150 evaluated programs, the mean best score increases with the swarm size. From the 55th program on, SwarmEvolve with 75 agents has the highest mean best score of all settings and baselines. The three baselines evaluate 80 to 160 programs in 60 minutes, and their final scores lie below the final score of every swarm size. After about 150 programs, the gains fall within the bootstrap intervals. Smaller swarms run faster, so they evaluate more programs in the 60-minute budget and their scores keep rising for longer. All four settings end the hour at similar scores. The early gain suggests that larger swarm examines each program from more perspectives, so its summarizer draws on more diverse ideas. The later convergence likely reflects the limits of the LLM itself. Since all latent agents share their knowledge, additional agents cant find the blind spots that earlier agents overlook, and the diversity gain saturates. larger model does raise the final score as shown in Table 1. Latent reasoning instead of text reasoning. Text reasoning takes most of the GPU time of all three baselines, 20 to 35 seconds and several thousand tokens per evaluated program. SwarmEvolve replaces it with latent reasoning and latent communication, which together take about tenth of its GPU time: the latent agents of round reason for few seconds in total. SwarmEvolve therefore spends most of its GPU time writing programs, and this shift explains its higher throughput. 2. Novelty check in latent space. To check novelty, ShinkaEvolve embeds the code of each new program with separate embedding model and, when its cosine similarity to an archived program exceeds 0.99, asks the LLM whether the two programs differ. These extra LLM calls take several minutes of 18 SwarmEvolve each run. The novelty filter of SwarmEvolve instead compares the mean hidden states of the latent agents, which are already in GPU memory, and takes seconds per run.

We implement SwarmEvolve in PyTorch with the Qwen3 models of Hugging Face Transformers [72]. The latent agents of round run as one batch, and latent agents that read the same program attend to one shared copy of its KV cache through the paged FlashAttention kernel of vLLM [18, 41]. The summarizers of round decode as one batch with paged KV caches and prompt-lookup speculative sampling, which drafts tokens by copying them from the programs in the context [57] and verifies them with the acceptance rule of speculative sampling, so the samples follow the distribution of the model exactly [44]. With Qwen3 14B and 32B-FP8, SwarmEvolve also captures its decoding steps in CUDA graphs and uses the fused kernels of vLLM, including FlashAttention-3 on the H100 GPU [58]. The three baselines serve the model with vLLM, which batches requests continuously, caches shared prefixes, and runs CUDA graphs, so their decoding runs at the speed of production serving engine. CodeEvolve runs its configuration for Qwen models with eight islands, one per CPU core. All four frameworks run Qwen3 32B-FP8, which uses the FP8 weights released by Qwen.

sections.title: D Benchmark Problems
sections.content: The 16 mathematical problems in Sections D.1D.16 are those of Appendix of AlphaEvolve [50], with the problem statements, initial programs, and evaluators of OpenEvolve [59]; the problem statement of circle packing in the unit square comes from ShinkaEvolve [42]. All feasibility checks use the numerical tolerances of the OpenEvolve evaluators. construction with objective value scores v/vAE, or vAE/v for minimization, where vAE is the exact value of AlphaEvolves published construction,1 so score above 1 improves on AlphaEvolve. Where an evaluator divides by rounded vAE, we rescale its scores to the exact value. We also design the 5 scientific computing problems in Sections D.17D.21. sections.content: Supplementary Table 5 lists the objective values behind the scores of Table 1: the value of AlphaEvolves published construction, the best value of the three runs of each framework, and the best known value. We rerun the best program of every run and recompute its value under AlphaEvolves exact constraints. For the programs that reproduce their logged score, the exact constraints lower the score by at most 3.3 104. The remaining programs draw unseeded random numbers, so we rerun each of them 33 times (once without seed and with seeds 0 to 31) and report the best value under the exact constraints among the reruns that the evaluator scores no higher than the logged score of the run. We call best known value verified if its construction or certificate has been checked, and claimed otherwise. With Qwen3 8B and 32B-FP8, SwarmEvolve improves on AlphaEvolve on the same three problems: it matches the best known packing of 26 circles in the unit square [62], and its step functions improve AlphaEvolves bounds on the second and third autocorrelation inequalities. The three baselines improve on AlphaEvolve only on the autocorrelation inequalities. Two problems need care in the comparison with AlphaEvolve. On the third autocorrelation inequality, the evaluator of OpenEvolve takes the absolute value of the autoconvolution inside the maximum, while AlphaEvolves published bound of 1.4557 takes it outside the maximum. Under the definition of the evaluator, AlphaEvolves construction gives 1.4688, the value that we compare against (Appendix D.12). On the uncertainty inequality, the evaluator accepts only functions built from Hermite polynomials. Within this family, AlphaEvolves first construction gives 0.3521, while its best bound of 0.3216 uses Laguerre polynomials, which lie outside the family. SwarmEvolve reaches 0.3521 with Qwen3 32B-FP8, the value of AlphaEvolves construction within the same family. With Qwen3 32B-FP8, SwarmEvolve comes close to AlphaEvolve on four more problems: within one part per million on circles in rectangle, and within 0.02% on the two distance ratios and the minimum overlap problem. sections.title: F Best Solutions Found by Each Framework
sections.content: We compare the best program that each framework found with Qwen3 8B for one packing problem, one geometry problem, and the three PDE problems. For each framework, the highest-scoring program is selected. For the PDE problems, we plot the pointwise absolute error uref, where is each frameworks solution and uref is the reference solution, on the same logarithmic scale for all three problems. 32 SwarmEvolve F.1 Circle Packing in the Unit Square Supplementary Figure 16 shows the best packing of each framework. Our method. The program runs ten restarts of one SLSQP optimization over all centers and radii, each from 16 perturbed lattice positions and 10 random positions, and keeps the best valid packing. OpenEvolve. The program places one circle at the center, eight on an inner ring, four in the corners, and thirteen on an outer ring, and optimizes all centers and radii with one SLSQP run. ShinkaEvolve. The program places one circle at the center, eight on an inner ring, thirteen on an outer ring clipped to the square, and four near the corners, and optimizes all centers and radii with one SLSQP run. CodeEvolve. The program places 25 circles on 5 5 lattice and one at the center, and optimizes all centers and radii with one SLSQP run. Supplementary Figure 16: Best packings of 26 circles in the unit square. The sums of the radii are 2.636 (our method), 2.615 (OpenEvolve), 2.626 (ShinkaEvolve), and 2.614 (CodeEvolve). F.2 Heilbronn Problem in Triangle Supplementary Figure 17 shows the best placement of each framework. Our method. The program runs ten restarts of simulated annealing from symmetric lattice of points, moving one point at time and accepting worse smallest area with probability that decreases as the temperature drops. OpenEvolve. The program draws 11 random points in the triangle, redrawing point whenever it is collinear with two earlier points. ShinkaEvolve. The program draws random configurations from 50 fixed seeds, keeps the best ones, and refines them with SLSQP on the smallest triangle area under the three edge constraints of the triangle. CodeEvolve. The program draws 11 random points in the triangle and runs one simulated annealing of 50,000 steps that moves one point at time. 33 SwarmEvolve Supplementary Figure 17: Best placements of 11 points in the equilateral triangle. The shaded triangle has the smallest area among all triangles formed by the points. The smallest areas, divided by the area of the triangle, are 0.0223 (our method), 0.0016 (OpenEvolve), 0.0200 (ShinkaEvolve), and 0.0222 (CodeEvolve). F.3 Viscous Burgers Equation Supplementary Figure 18 shows the solution of each framework for the smallest viscosity and its error. Our method. The program uses central finite differences on 8192 grid points for ν < 0.01 and 2048 points otherwise, with two-stage RungeKutta method and time step limited by both the advection and the diffusion stability conditions. OpenEvolve. The program uses central finite differences of the flux u2/2 on 2048 grid points with forward Euler time steps. ShinkaEvolve. The program splits each time step into two-stage RungeKutta step for the advection on 1024 grid points and an implicit diffusion step solved exactly in Fourier space. CodeEvolve. The program uses central finite differences of the flux u2/2 on 1024 grid points with the explicit midpoint method, two-stage RungeKutta method, and time step limited by both the advection and the diffusion stability conditions. 34 SwarmEvolve Supplementary Figure 18: Solutions u(x, 1) of the Burgers equation for ν = 0.001 (top) and their absolute errors (bottom). Our solution is the most accurate away from the shock at = 0. F.4 Convection-Diffusion Equation Supplementary Figure 19 shows the solution of each framework for ε = 103 and its error. Our method. The program uses central finite differences on 768 768 grid with sparse direct solver and bilinear interpolation to the evaluation points. OpenEvolve. The program uses central finite differences on 512 512 grid with sparse direct solver and bilinear interpolation. ShinkaEvolve. The program uses central finite differences on 512 512 grid with sparse direct solver and bilinear interpolation. CodeEvolve. The program uses central finite differences on 128 128 grid with sparse direct solver and bilinear interpolation. 35 SwarmEvolve Supplementary Figure 19: Solutions of the convection-diffusion equation for ε = 103 (top) and their absolute errors (bottom). The errors concentrate in the boundary layers along = 1 and = 1 and along the characteristic line from the corner (0, 0). The coarser grid of CodeEvolve spreads the error near = 1 over wider region. F.5 Helmholtz Equation Supplementary Figure 20 shows the solution of each framework for = 40 and its error. Our method. The program uses second-order finite differences with ghost points for the impedance condition on an 818 818 grid, sparse direct solver, and bilinear interpolation. OpenEvolve. The program uses the same discretization on 301 301 grid. ShinkaEvolve. The program uses the same discretization on 601 601 grid. CodeEvolve. The program uses the same discretization on 401 401 grid and smooths the real and imaginary parts of the solution with Gaussian filter. 36 SwarmEvolve Supplementary Figure 20: Real parts of the solutions of the Helmholtz equation for = 40 (top) and their absolute errors (bottom). The error decreases with the number of grid points per wavelength.

sections.title: G Evolution Trajectories
sections.content: Supplementary Figure 21 plots the best score so far against wall-clock minutes for each problem and framework with Qwen3 8B, and Supplementary Figures 22 and 23 show the same with Qwen3 14B and 32B-FP8. Each line averages the three runs of framework, and each band spans its lowest and highest run. With every model, the curves of SwarmEvolve rise most steeply in the first minutes, when its rounds explore many focuses at once, and end the hour highest on most problems. Its bands often lie entirely above those of the baselines, so its lead holds for every seed. 37 SwarmEvolve Supplementary Figure 21: Best score so far against wall-clock minutes for each problem with Qwen3 8B. Each line is the best score so far averaged over three runs, and each band spans the lowest and highest run. SwarmEvolve ends the hour with the highest score on 18 of the 21 problems, and its curves rise most steeply in the first few minutes. 38 SwarmEvolve Supplementary Figure 22: Best score so far against wall-clock minutes for each problem with Qwen3 14B. Each line is the best score so far averaged over three runs, and each band spans the lowest and highest run. SwarmEvolve ends the hour with the highest or tied-highest score on 16 of the 21 problems. 39 SwarmEvolve Supplementary Figure 23: Best score so far against wall-clock minutes for each problem with Qwen3 32BFP8. Each line is the best score so far averaged over three runs, and each band spans the lowest and highest run. SwarmEvolve ends the hour with the highest or tied-highest score on 17 of the 21 problems.
